summary: Extend the standard columnar algorithm to whole numbers with more than four digits. The procedure is identical to four-digit work (align by place value, compose when carrying, decompose when borrowing), but larger scale raises the stakes: subtracting from a large round number such as 500,000 − 234,178 forces an exchange that cascades across several zeros, and adding three or more five-digit numbers can produce carries greater than one. Estimation-first and inverse checking matter more because a single misaligned digit is now worth thousands.
misconceptions: Extended borrow-across-zero fails — cannot cascade an exchange through several zeros (500,000 - 234,178)
Smaller-from-larger bug persists at larger scale
Misaligns digits when numbers have different lengths
When a column totals 20+ (three addends), carries only 1 instead of 2
Checks by redoing rather than estimating or using the inverse

activities.title: Borrowing across a row of zeros (500,000 − 234,178)
steps: Set out 500,000 − 234,178 in columns aligned by place value, from the ones on the right.
Before computing, estimate by rounding (about 500,000 − 234,000 = 266,000) and note the expected size of the answer.

At the ones there is nothing to take 8 from, and every column to the left is 0; work the exchange by taking one hundred-thousand and walking it down column by column so each 0 becomes 9 as a ten is passed along, until the ones finally hold 10.
Check with the inverse: 265,822 + 234,178 should return 500,000, and compare to your estimate (~266,000).
Optionally model the same subtraction as counting up on an empty number line — jump from 234,178 up to 500,000 and total the jumps — as an independent alternative that should also give 265,822.
Optionally repeat with an easier round-number case such as 500,000 − 234,000 and discuss why that borrow is simpler.
activities.insight: A single exchange can cascade through a row of zeros — each zero becomes a 9 as the ten is passed along, and the ones finally hold 10 — so a wall of zeros is not a dead end.

activities.title: Adding three numbers of up to five digits: when the carry is more than one
steps: Set out 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058 in a single column layout, aligning by place value from the ones on the right (numbers of different lengths must still line up); optionally show the three addends as parts of a part-whole bar whose whole is the total.
Add the ones column aloud and name the full total (0 + 6 + 8 = 14): write 4, carry 1.

Work through the rest of this sum: note that every carry here is only 1 (column totals including carries: tens 10, hundreds 11, thousands 16; the ten-thousands totals 3 with no carry), finishing at 36,104. This is good practice at keeping three different-length addends aligned and tracking repeated carries.

Now tackle a case that genuinely produces a larger carry, e.g. 36,489 + 27,858 + 15,937: the ones column totals 9 + 8 + 7 = 24, so write 4 and carry 2 (not 1); completing it gives 80,284, with several columns (ones, hundreds and thousands) carrying 2.
Compute 34,567 + 28,945 = 63,512 as a clean two-addend check that the basic algorithm is intact.
Estimate by rounding before computing so a place-value slip in the thousands or ten-thousands is caught.
activities.insight: When a column of three or more addends totals 20 or more, the carry can be 2 (or more), not automatically 1. (Not every three-addend sum reaches that — 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058 only ever carries 1 — so a case whose column actually totals into the twenties is needed to surface the larger carry.)

activities.title: Worked-example reference and estimate-then-check routine
steps: Study a tap-to-reveal or step-by-step worked example of the across-many-zeros borrow, revealing each 0-becomes-9 exchange in turn to see the cascade clearly.
For every large calculation, first write a rounded estimate, then compute, then compare the answer to the estimate.
Check subtractions with the inverse addition (or a counting-up number line) and additions with an estimate rather than by redoing the same calculation.

Answer prompts: roughly how big should 500,000 − 234,178 be before working it out? Why did all those zeros turn into 9s? Would 500,000 − 234,000 be easier to borrow, and why? Why carry 2 and not 1 when a three-addend column totals into the twenties?
activities.insight: Estimating first and checking by the inverse catch place-value slips that are now worth thousands; redoing the same method just reproduces the same error.

checkQuestion: Give the child three to set out and solve on paper, watching alignment and exchange: 34,567 + 28,945; 500,000 - 234,178; and add these three in one column: 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058. Then ask them to check the subtraction by estimating and by the inverse.
checkAnswer: 34,567 + 28,945 = 63,512 (composes through the columns). 500,000 - 234,178 = 265,822, cascading one exchange through the zeros. The three-addend sum = 36,104, carrying 2 where a column totals 20+. Estimate for the subtraction approx 500,000 - 234,000 = 266,000, close to 265,822; inverse 265,822 + 234,178 = 500,000.
